summary: The revision makes real security work the core: read-only M365 checks, external scans and an annual test replace owner self-attestation and the risky incident engine. But a monthly findings email is too slow to catch BEC. Pen-test scope skips workstations and remote access, where tax offices get breached. A multi-tenant app with standing read access to many financial firms concentrates risk.

objections.objection: The monitor reports by monthly email, but the signals it collects are attacks in progress. An external forwarding rule, a new Global Admin or a risky sign-in means business email compromise is happening now. Learning about it up to 30 days later is post-mortem evidence, not detection. On Entra ID Free tenants (Business Basic/Standard), sign-in and audit logs are kept for only 7 days, so a monthly pull misses most activity unless the product polls daily and stores the data. It needs near-real-time alerts to the owner and MSP for high-severity changes, and daily collection, or it does not reduce BEC risk or meaningfully address 314.4(c)(8) user-activity monitoring.
objections.evidence: concept:mvp.features[1] ('monthly findings email'); https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/monitoring-health/reference-reports-data-retention (Free: sign-ins and audit logs 7 days)

objections.objection: The penetration test covers only 'internet-facing services and the M365 tenant', within a budget of about 8 founder hours per client per year that must also cover two scans, a tabletop and the report. Small tax and mortgage offices usually expose almost nothing externally. Their real compromise paths are phishing, infostealers or remote-access tools on workstations, shared local admin accounts, and tax or LOS software on office PCs. A test that never touches endpoints or the internal network produces a clean dated report while the main attack surface goes untested. That is checkbox compliance, the problem round 1 flagged in a new form, and an incident on an untested workstation would expose it.
objections.evidence: concept:mvp.features[2] (scope: internet-facing services and M365 tenant); concept:build.hardest_parts[2] (~8 hours/year per Program client); https://www.ecfr.gov/api/renderer/v1/content/enhanced/current/title-16?part=314&section=314.4 ((d)(2)(i) testing 'of your information systems ... based on relevant identified risks')

objections.objection: The checks the concept lists need tenant-wide application permissions: AuditLog.Read.All for sign-ins, MailboxSettings.Read for inbox rules on every mailbox, Policy/Directory reads, and app-only Exchange Online access for forwarding. These permissions stay granted indefinitely across dozens of financial firms' tenants. One stolen app secret or certificate, or a compromise of the founder's laptop, becomes a read path into every client and a ready map of their weaknesses (the findings database). Attackers have abused OAuth apps this way before. A solo founder running the platform with no 24/7 coverage is a concentrated supply-chain risk. MSPs and the 314.4(f) oversight duty will ask for evidence the concept does not yet plan: certificate auth held in an HSM or Key Vault, per-tenant app registrations or GDAP, Conditional Access for workload identities, an independent assessment, and a breach notification commitment.

Risk detections need Entra ID P1 or P2, and Business Basic/Standard tenants have neither. Risky sign-ins are kept for only 7 days on Free. On the cheaper tenants many of these offices run, 'risky sign-ins' will mostly be empty. The monitor then shrinks to configuration checks (MFA, admins, forwarding, stale accounts). The product should say so per tenant, and perhaps recommend Business Premium as a finding.

The configuration checks repeat what MSPs already run for free. Maester, CISA ScubaGear, Microsoft Secure Score and Lighthouse cover MFA, admin roles and forwarding, Maester with thousands of read-only checks mapped to CIS/CISA that never leave the tenant. A competent MSP will see the monitor as a lighter version of tools it has and value only the Safeguards mapping, the testing and the reports. A third-party vendor's findings may also conflict with these tools' results.

strongest_point: Founder-delivered six-monthly scans and an annual test, combined with read-only M365 checks, give small offices real evidence of configuration and the (d)(2) deliverable that WISP vendors never provide.
what_would_change_my_mind: The monitor collects data daily and sends same-day alerts for external forwarding, new privileged roles and MFA removal; a 10-tenant pilot detects and contains at least one real or simulated BEC indicator within 24 hours.

The pen-test scope includes an authenticated internal and endpoint review (local admins, remote-access tools, EDR presence, patch levels) plus a phishing-resilience check, and a time study shows it fits the hours budget or the price is raised to cover it.

A documented vendor security design (certificate credentials in an HSM or Key Vault, per-tenant isolation or GDAP, least-privilege scopes listed, workload-identity Conditional Access, an external review) that two MSPs accept in their vendor assessment.
MSPs already running Maester or ScubaGear say in pilots that the Safeguards mapping and testing are worth reselling on top.

resolved_prior.objection: The program was mostly self-attested paperwork with no technical verification of M365, Google or endpoints.
resolved_prior.note: A read-only Graph/Exchange monitor for MFA, leavers, forwarding, admin roles and risky sign-ins is now the core feature. Its monthly cadence and licence limits remain new issues.

resolved_prior.objection: The program omitted the 314.4(c)(8) monitoring/logging and (d)(2) testing controls.
resolved_prior.note: The six-monthly external scans and annual test meet (d)(2) on paper. (c)(8) is only partly covered: a monthly pull of 7-day logs is not user-activity monitoring, and the test scope is narrow (see new objections).

resolved_prior.objection: The incident clock asked owners forensic questions that decide reportability and could produce a confidently wrong 'not reportable' record.
resolved_prior.note: Reportability reasoning was removed. The card presumes reportability, routes to the insurer or counsel and records facts only.

resolved_prior.objection: Insurer breach counsel would sideline a non-privileged third-party incident timeline.
resolved_prior.note: The record is now facts-only handoff material to the breach coach. The insurer hotline comes first.

resolved_prior.objection: Owner-run PowerShell hardening risks lockouts, makes the vendor a privileged third party, and the vendor's own security posture was missing.
resolved_prior.note: Scripts were removed and changes need separate written authorization. Vendor security is now listed as a hardest part, but standing multi-tenant read access raises a larger concentration risk (new objection).

resolved_prior.objection: The marketing overstated duties for firms under 5,000 consumers that 314.6 exempts.
resolved_prior.note: Scoping at onboarding, resegmentation to 5,000+ consumers, and a Core tier labelled as good practice.
